title: How to turn off smart quotes in Word for Mac, and fix quotes already typed
metaTitle: Turn off smart quotes in Word for Mac, plus fixes for old text
description: Turn off smart quotes in Word for Mac from AutoFormat As You Type, then fix curly quotes already in your file with Find and Replace.
targetKeyword: how to turn off smart quotes in Word for Mac
secondaryKeywords: turn off smart quotes Mac system setting
intro: To turn off smart quotes in Word for Mac, open Word > Preferences > AutoCorrect, click AutoFormat As You Type, and clear the box for “Straight quotes” with “smart quotes.” That stops new curly quotes. It does not change quotes already in your file, so you also need Find and Replace, and a copy of the file in case something goes wrong.
tldr: Clear the “Straight quotes” with “smart quotes” box on the AutoFormat As You Type tab to stop new curly quotes.
That setting only affects new typing. Old curly quotes stay until you replace them.
Run Find and Replace on a copy, then read the first matches before you save over the original.
Apple’s system setting, Use smart quotes and dashes, may cover other Mac apps, but not all of them.

blocks.text: Turn off smart quotes in Word for Mac

Start with the setting that creates the marks. Word swaps straight quotes for curly ones as you type, and the switch sits on the AutoFormat As You Type tab. Menu names move between Word releases, so your screen may differ slightly. If it does, look for AutoCorrect in the Word menu and work from there.

items: Click Word in the menu bar, then choose Preferences.
Choose AutoCorrect. If you don’t see it, try Tools > AutoCorrect Options.
Click the AutoFormat As You Type tab.
Under Replace as you type, find the box labeled “Straight quotes” with “smart quotes.”
Clear the box so it has no check mark, then click OK.
Type a word inside quote marks in a blank document to test it.

blocks.title: Check it with a test line
blocks.text: Type a short word inside quote marks in a blank document. If the marks stay straight, the setting is off. Delete the test line afterward, so it doesn’t end up in your draft.
Why the setting does not fix old text

This is the part that trips people up. The AutoFormat switch only affects what you type from now on. Microsoft’s support page describes the change as happening as you type. It says nothing about text already in the file. Pasted text keeps the marks it arrived with, so a long draft can end up with both kinds.
Convert the quotes you already have

Find and Replace handles the file you already wrote. A Microsoft Q&A thread describes a 170-page document in Word for Mac 16.68 that mixed straight and curly marks from pasted text. The original poster reported 965 quote marks updated after one Replace All. The thread does not say which mark style the poster wanted in the end, and it does not explain how Word matches curly marks against a straight search. Treat it as a method to test, not a promise.

The thread’s method is simple. Two things I would add are a test copy and a check of the first matches. Turning AutoFormat off first means the marks you type into the boxes should stay straight. Confirm that with a test line before you rely on it.

items: Save a copy of the file under a new name.
Choose Edit > Find > Advanced Find and Replace.
Turn AutoFormat off first, as described above, then click into the boxes.
Type the straight double quote key into the Find box, then into the Replace box.
Click Replace All. Repeat with the straight apostrophe key in both boxes for single quotes.
Read the first matches in the document before you save over the original.

blocks.text: A worked example on a long report

Say you have a long report with quotes pasted from interviews, plus one code sample that needs straight marks to run. Start by selecting the code sample and cutting it into a scratch document. That keeps the global replace away from it. Run the double quote pass on the prose first, then read the first matches to confirm the direction.

Next, run the apostrophe pass on the prose. Scan the results for words like don’t and the possessive forms, since those are the most common apostrophes in pasted text. When the prose looks right, paste the code sample back in. Check it once more by reading it, because a straight mark that turned curly will break a command.

blocks.title: Watch for code and measurements
blocks.text: A global replace also touches code samples, file paths, and measurements. Those parts may need straight marks on purpose. Scan them by hand before you run Replace All, and edit them separately if they need to stay as they are.
Does the Mac system setting cover Word?

Apple also has a switch for the whole Mac. Go to Apple menu > System Settings > Keyboard > Text Input > Edit, then turn “Use smart quotes and dashes” on or off and click Done. Apple’s guide warns that smart quotes aren’t available in all apps. Treat the system switch as a starting point, then check each app on its own.

Apple does not list which apps follow the switch. I could not confirm whether Word follows it, so don’t assume it does. Word’s own AutoFormat setting is the one to change first. To convert existing text in Mac apps that support it, select the text and choose Edit > Substitutions > Show Substitutions. Make sure the Smart Dashes and Smart Quotes boxes are selected, then click Replace in Selection, or Replace All for the whole document. Apple’s guide describes this for smart quotes, so check the result on a sample first.

blocks.text: Why straight quotes turn curly in the first place

Straight quotes are a typewriter habit, according to a typography guide written for lawyers. A typewriter used one key for both opening and closing quotes. Word and Mac text settings now separate the two. They swap in curly marks as you type, which looks polished in most prose. It becomes a problem when you need straight marks for code, plain text, or a house style.

Mixed marks usually come from somewhere else. Text copied from a web page, an email, or a PDF carries its own quote characters. Pasting it into Word brings those characters along. In the Q&A case, the AutoFormat setting did not fix the pasted text. That is why one file can show straight and curly quotes side by side.
Does the wrong quote style hurt your writing?

No study I found measures how often writers hit quote problems, or what those problems cost in time or grades. Treat any claim about quote style as a judgment call. The closest evidence is about spelling errors. A 2022 online experiment with 100 English speakers rated short health-forum excerpts. Two spelling errors cut the trust rating by 5.91 points on a 0 to 100 scale. Five errors cut it by 13.5 points.

Quote marks are not spelling errors. A reader may never notice a curly mark. Publishers often care more. Chicago’s Shop Talk blog says smart marks are preferred for published work, while straight marks are fine for correspondence and social media. Sources disagree on the details, so check the style guide your editor or publisher uses.
Mistakes people make when they turn it off

items: Turning the setting off and expecting old quotes to change. They stay until you replace them.
Replacing marks across a whole file when only one section needs it.
Forgetting apostrophes. Single quotes need their own pass.
Running a global replace on code, file paths, or inch marks.
Skipping the copy. A bad replace is harder to undo across a long file.
Assuming Word, Pages, and Google Docs share one setting.

blocks.text: Pages and Google Docs need their own check

Pages is an Apple app, but Apple warns that smart quotes aren’t available in every app. Type a sample line in Pages and check which marks appear. For Google Docs, the official autocorrect help page describes Tools > Preferences > Substitutions. It does not name a smart quotes option, so look at that tab yourself and read what’s there.
Where Lazur helps, and where it doesn’t

Lazur is a voice assistant for the Mac. Hold ⌥ ⌘ to ask about anything on screen, and it answers out loud. Ask where the setting is, and Lazur draws a circle and a label around it. Ask how to change it, and Lazur guides you one click at a time, waiting for each click. It does not click for you.

Lazur is not a plugin or add-in for Word. It won’t decide which quotes should change. You still choose the replace, read the results, and save the file. Lazur runs on macOS only. See /pricing for plans and the free trial.

For a writer, the useful part is the setting hunt and the checking. Ask Lazur to point at the AutoFormat tab, then move at your own pace. If you write long drafts, [Word for writers on Mac](/for/writers/word) covers templates and dictation in more depth.
Keep straight quotes from coming back

Settings can differ on a new Mac or a fresh Word install, so check the box at the start of each project. Put a line in your template or project notes that names the quote style your file needs. Lazur can draft that note for you, or you can set an Apple Reminders alert before you export or submit.

A short file needs one pass with AutoFormat off and a quick read. A long file needs a copy, a test on one sample section, and a read of the first matches before you save. That order catches a wrong direction early, before it spreads across the file.

faq.question: Does turning off smart quotes fix quotes already in my Word document?
faq.answer: No. The AutoFormat As You Type switch affects new typing. Existing curly quotes stay until you replace them with Find and Replace on a copy of the file.

faq.question: Where is the smart quotes setting in Word for Mac?
faq.answer: Look under Word > Preferences > AutoCorrect, then the AutoFormat As You Type tab. Menu names differ by release. Some Microsoft community answers use Tools > AutoCorrect Options instead.

faq.question: Will turning off the Mac system setting change Word?
faq.answer: I could not confirm that Word follows Apple’s setting. Apple says smart quotes aren’t available in all apps. Change Word’s own AutoFormat setting, then test it with a sample line.

faq.question: Should I use straight quotes in a published document?
faq.answer: It depends on the publisher. Chicago’s Shop Talk blog prefers smart marks for published work. It calls straight marks fine for correspondence and social media. Check your editor’s or publisher’s style guide before you decide.

faq.question: Do apostrophes change too?
faq.answer: They can, but a double quote search does not cover them. Run a separate pass for single quotes, using the straight apostrophe key in both the Find and Replace boxes.

faq.question: Can Lazur turn off smart quotes for me?
faq.answer: No. Lazur does not click buttons or change settings for you. It can point at the AutoFormat tab, draw a circle around the checkbox, and guide you one click at a time.

faq.question: Does Google Docs use the same setting?
faq.answer: No. Google Docs has its own autocorrect preferences. Google’s help page describes Tools > Preferences > Substitutions but does not name a smart quotes option, so check that dialog yourself.

faq.question: Should I replace quotes in code?
faq.answer: Usually not. Code often needs straight marks. Scan code blocks, file paths, and measurements by hand before you run a global replace.

costs.title: Hours of cleanup in a long file
costs.text: In the Microsoft Q&A case, one user faced a 170-page file with mixed marks from pasted text. Fixing them by hand would be slow. A single Find and Replace pass is faster, but only after you test it on a copy. The real cost is the time you spend checking results, and no study I found has measured it.

costs.title: Reader trust, in a small way
costs.text: The best evidence I found is about spelling, not quotes. Two spelling errors cut a trust rating by 5.91 points in a 2022 experiment. Quote marks were not part of that test, so the number does not transfer directly. Treat it as a hint, not a measurement of quote style.

costs.title: A mismatch with a publisher’s style
costs.text: Chicago’s Shop Talk blog says smart marks are preferred for published work. An editor who expects curly marks may still flag straight ones, or the reverse. The cost shows up when your file goes to someone who follows a different guide, so check that guide before you start.

costs.title: Broken code, paths, and measurements
costs.text: A global replace can change quote marks in places where they matter. Code samples, file paths, and measurements may need straight marks to work. Fixing a broken code sample after a replace costs more time than a careful scan before you run it.

causes.title: A typewriter habit
causes.text: Straight quotes are a typewriter habit, according to a typography guide written for lawyers. The typewriter had one key for both opening and closing quotes. Word and Mac text settings separate the two now, so they swap in curly marks as you type.

causes.title: Word swaps marks as you type
causes.text: The AutoFormat As You Type setting converts straight quotes into curly ones while you type. New text often comes out curly without you noticing. The switch only changes typing from that point forward, so older text keeps whatever marks it already had.

causes.title: Pasted text brings its own marks
causes.text: Text from a web page, an email, or a PDF can carry curly quote characters. Pasting it into Word keeps them. The AutoFormat switch does not clean up pasted text, which is why a single file can show both kinds of quotes.

causes.title: Mac-wide text settings
causes.text: Apple has a system switch called Use smart quotes and dashes. It affects text typed into apps that follow it. Apple’s guide says the feature is not available in every app, so the same text can behave differently from one app to the next.

causes.title: Apps with their own rules
causes.text: Word, Pages, and Google Docs each keep their own autocorrect and substitution settings. Check each app on its own. A file that moves between apps may pick up different marks at each stop, so look at it again after a move.

fixes.title: Turn off AutoFormat As You Type in Word
fixes.text: Open Word > Preferences > AutoCorrect, click the AutoFormat As You Type tab, and clear the box for “Straight quotes” with “smart quotes.” Click OK. Then type a word inside quote marks in a blank document to confirm the marks stay straight.

fixes.title: Replace existing marks on a copy
fixes.text: Save a copy first. Then choose Edit > Find > Advanced Find and Replace, type the straight double quote key into both boxes, and click Replace All. Repeat for single quotes. Read the first matches before you keep the result.

fixes.title: Check the Mac system setting
fixes.text: Go to Apple menu > System Settings > Keyboard > Text Input > Edit. Turn “Use smart quotes and dashes” on or off, then click Done. Test each app you use, because Apple warns the setting does not apply in every app.

fixes.title: Use Substitutions in Mac text apps
fixes.text: In apps that support it, select the text and choose Edit > Substitutions > Show Substitutions. Make sure the Smart Dashes and Smart Quotes boxes are selected, then click Replace in Selection or Replace All. Apple describes this method, so check the result on a sample first.

fixes.title: Check Google Docs preferences
fixes.text: Google’s autocorrect help page describes Tools > Preferences > Substitutions. The page does not name a smart quotes option, so open that tab, read the options, and test a sample line. Do not rely on a guide that you cannot verify.

fixes.title: Scan code and measurements by hand
fixes.text: Before any global replace, read code blocks, file paths, and measurements. Those parts may need straight marks to work. Fix them in a separate pass, or leave them alone, so the replace does not break them.

plan.label: Day 1
plan.title: Turn the setting off
plan.text: Open Word > Preferences > AutoCorrect, clear the straight quotes box on the AutoFormat As You Type tab, then type a test word in a blank document. Confirm the marks stay straight before you open any real file.

plan.label: Day 2
plan.title: Test on a copy
plan.text: Duplicate the file you need to fix. In the copy, run Find and Replace for the double quote, then for the apostrophe. Read the first matches to confirm the direction before you touch the original.

plan.label: Day 3
plan.title: Scan the risky parts
plan.text: Check code blocks, file paths, and measurements by hand. Fix those sections separately, so the global replace does not change them by accident.

plan.text: Type a sample line in Pages and in Google Docs. See which marks appear in each. Change those settings if the same problem shows up there too.
